source.citation: Butler G, Baker J, Amend SR, Pienta KJ, Venditti C. No evidence for Peto’s paradox in terrestrial vertebrates. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2025;122(9):e2422861122

statement.value: Here, we show that there is no evidence for Peto’s paradox across amphibians, birds, mammals, and squamate reptiles: Larger species do in fact have a higher cancer prevalence compared to smaller species.

explanandum.value: Peto’s paradox—the puzzling disconnect between body size and cancer prevalence across species—has long stood as one of comparative biology’s most captivating and unresolved enigmas.

summary.value: The mix of substrates used by natural selection to sculpt and shape species body size through time has also resulted in concomitant solutions (30) that stave off the growing threat of cancer as birds and mammals become ever larger.

scope.value: Neoplastic and malignant prevalence paired with body size in 263 species of four vertebrate classes (31 amphibians, 79 birds, 90 mammals and 63 squamate reptiles). Snout–vent length is used as a proxy for body mass in amphibians and squamate reptiles, owing to the sparsity of body mass information for them; amphibians and reptiles are analysed separately from birds and mammals to account for potential differences in growth dynamics (determinate vs indeterminate growth). The association is estimated after accounting for the number of necropsies per species, with 11 outlier species removed. The prevalence data come from animals under managed care: they were aggregated from zoological institutions, aquariums and other facilities.

statement.value: Across amphibians, birds, mammals and squamate reptiles, larger species have a higher prevalence of neoplasia than smaller species after accounting for the number of necropsies per species: neoplasia is positively associated with snout–vent length in amphibians and squamate reptiles and with body mass in birds and mammals.

modality.basis_quote: Across all four vertebrate classes, larger species have an increased prevalence of neoplasia compared to smaller species.

statement.value: Across amphibians, birds, mammals and squamate reptiles, larger species have a higher prevalence of malignancy than smaller species after accounting for the number of necropsies per species: malignancy is positively associated with snout–vent length in amphibians and squamate reptiles and with body mass in birds and mammals.

modality.basis_quote: Across all four vertebrate classes, larger species have an increased prevalence of malignancy compared to smaller species, thus demonstrating no evidence of Peto’s paradox.

statement.value: The associations with body size are not attributable to species longevity: longevity was not a significant predictor of neoplasia or malignancy in amphibians and squamate reptiles or in birds and mammals, although more expansive longevity data are required to fully elucidate its effect.

modality.basis_quote: Thus, these findings cannot be attributed to species longevity.

statement.value: In birds and mammals, species that underwent more total body size evolution (a higher pathwise rate) have a lower prevalence of neoplasia and malignancy at the same present-day body size; in amphibians and squamate reptiles, pathwise rate was not a significant predictor of either.

modality.basis_quote: This means that birds and mammals that underwent more total body size evolution have a decreased prevalence of neoplasia and malignancy even if their present-day body size is the same.

statement.value: In birds and mammals, high rates of body size evolution may reflect the evolution of superior anticancer mechanisms: once the rate of historic body size evolution is accounted for, neoplasia and malignancy prevalence increase more steeply with species size.

modality.basis_quote: supporting the hypothesis that high rates of body size evolution may reflect the evolution of more superior anticancer mechanisms

statement.value: The loss of regenerative tissue capabilities, which has been linked to the metabolic cost of endothermy in birds and mammals, may explain why high rates of body size evolution are not associated with malignancy prevalence in amphibians and reptiles: selection may have tightened cellular growth control in birds and mammals but only tuned it in amphibians and reptiles to allow regeneration.

modality.basis_quote: we speculate that this loss of this capability may also explain the lack of association between high rates of body size evolution and malignancy prevalence in amphibians and reptiles

falsification_condition.value: No association between malignancy and body size, after accounting for the number of necropsies per species, would count against the claim and for Peto’s paradox.
falsification_condition.basis_quote: If Peto’s paradox is true, we expect to find no association between malignancy and body size after accounting for the number of necropsies per species.

claim_or_ref.text: Evolutionary mismatch in captivity: the positive trends observed in data from captive animals may result from conditions in captivity (nutrition, exposure to pollution, parasites, physical activity) that differ from the natural environments in which the species evolved their anticancer defences; under those conditions Peto’s paradox could be partially refuted by an increased and artificial exposure to oncogenic risks.

value.unresolved_reason: Presented as possible, not as tested.

value.question: Prevalences aggregate many cancer types; does the positive trend between body mass and cancer risk across species hold for specific cancer types?

The number of necropsies varies greatly between species and prevalence is uncertain for species with few necropsies; with a different sampling, some trends could have had different directions and significance.
Do cancer trends in captive animals represent those of wild species and the oncogenic pressures for which their cancer suppression evolved?

value.observation: The Asian elephant (Elephas maximus), often touted as the quintessential example of Peto’s paradox, has a lower than expected prevalence of malignancy, but not an exceptionally low one.
Peto’s paradox, the absence of a positive association between cancer prevalence and body size across species, has remained one of the most elusive mysteries in comparative biology.

value.finding: Earlier tests across vertebrate classes reported a positive association between neoplasia and body size in some groups, but no study found an association between malignancy and body size.
value.current_interpretation: Malignancy does not increase with body size across species: the crux of Peto’s paradox.
value.proposed_interpretation: Those tests modelled the proportion of malignancy per necropsy for each species. High variation in malignancy between species makes this underestimate the relation with body size, and proportions do not evolve by Brownian motion; modelling the observed number of malignancies of each species directly avoids both problems.

value.new_question: Which defence mechanisms, or their absence, make species such as the naked mole rat (much lower malignancy than predicted) and the budgerigar (much higher) deviate from the prevalence expected from their body size and historic rate of body size evolution?
value.why_not_askable_today: A species is exceptional only relative to the malignancy prevalence expected from its body size and rate of body size evolution; these species were identified by comparing observed with predicted prevalence.
value.enabling_method: Comparison of observed malignancy prevalence with the prevalence predicted from body mass and pathwise rate, followed by mechanistic studies of malignancy defence in the outlying species.

value.justification: The claim is tested across a dataset spanning four vertebrate classes: after accounting for the number of necropsies per species, no association between malignancy and body size is expected if Peto’s paradox is true and a positive association if it is false.

cheapest_test.text: Test for an association between malignancy and body size after accounting for the number of necropsies per species, in a dataset spanning several vertebrate classes.

source_ref.limitation: The article itself; its full-text XML is hashed in author.source, not stored in this repository.

value.note: The claim that Peto’s paradox is not supported across the four classes is made in this article (paragraphs 3 and 5); the date is its publication date in the article metadata. The expectation that larger, longer-lived species have more cancer, and the paradox, are credited to Peto (1977) (paragraph 7). The article credits earlier work with reporting positive associations between neoplasia and body size in some vertebrate groups (its refs. 11 and 13, paragraph 8).

summary.value: Body size evolution is heterogeneous: some lineages have undergone more body size evolution than expected, likely under increased selective pressures, and body size evolution is associated with the evolution of other traits. The authors therefore might expect high rates of body size evolution also to reflect the evolution of better anticancer mechanisms: evolution favours larger-bodied animals, as expected under Cope’s rule, so those animals that get big would be expected to have developed superior mechanisms of cancer defence.

The passage gives no method for testing the urodele prediction, so it does not support the 'phylogenetic' part of the classification.

The passage gives grounds for system indirectness (non-avian sauropsids include turtles and crocodiles) but says nothing about the endpoint, so the endpoint rating of none is unsupported.

The passage supports a positive malignancy-body mass association only in Compton's mammals and amphibians and reports no significant association in birds or non-avian sauropsids, so it does not support the claim across all four classes.
